prompt: `int fine;` is declared, assigned only inside an `if`, then printed. What does `javac` say?
hint: The compiler follows paths, not values.

choices.text: Nothing; it prints 0 when the `if` does not run
choices.why: 0 is a field's default; a local has none, and the compiler refused the file.

choices.text: `variable fine might not have been initialized`
choices.why: Right: on the path where the `if` is skipped, `fine` has no value.

choices.text: A warning, and the program prints whatever was in memory
choices.why: That is what C does; Java makes it an error.

prompt: `daysLate` is 3, so the `if` in `Fine.java` always runs. Why does the compiler still refuse to print `fine`?
hint: What does the compiler look at?

choices.text: Because `daysLate` might change while the program runs
choices.why: Nothing changes it; the reason is that the compiler does not reason about values at all.

choices.text: It checks every path through the code, not the values on it
choices.why: Right: definite assignment is about every path, whatever the values.

choices.text: Because a variable declared without a value can never be assigned later
choices.why: It can; `fine = daysLate * 50;` is a valid assignment on the path that runs it.

prompt: Match each field type to the default `Defaults.java` printed.
hint: Zero, in some form, or nothing.

prompt: Why do fields get a default value while locals must be assigned before use?
hint: Who can read each one, and when?

choices.text: The compiler cannot follow every path to a field
choices.why: Right: a local is only seen inside its method, where every path can be checked.

choices.text: Fields are created by the JVM and locals by the compiler
choices.why: Both exist only while the program runs; the compiler checks rules, it creates no variables.

choices.text: Defaults are slower, so Java only spends them on fields
choices.why: Speed is not the reason; the compiler's reach is.

prompt: A `Member` class has a field `String email;` that nothing assigns. A method sends a reminder to `email`. What goes wrong, and when?
hint: Fields get a default, and the default for a `String` is not text.

choices.text: The compiler refuses the class, as it refused `Fine.java`
choices.why: That rule is for locals; a field compiles and starts as `null`.

choices.text: Nothing goes wrong; the reminder is sent to an empty address
choices.why: The default is `null`, not an empty string; there is no address at all.

choices.text: It compiles, and fails only when the program runs and uses the `null`
choices.why: Right: a default is a value nobody chose, and it looks like data until it is used.

prompt: The rule that a local must certainly have a value before it is read is called definite ___.
hint: The act of putting a value in a variable.

prompt: Where does the scope of a local variable end?
hint: Not the method: the block.

choices.text: At the end of the method
choices.why: A variable declared inside an `if` ended at the `if`'s brace, before the method did.

choices.text: At the closing brace of the block holding it
choices.why: Right: which is why `extra` meant nothing on line 9.

choices.text: At the end of the line that declares it
choices.why: Then no variable could be used on the next line.

choices.text: When the garbage collector removes it
choices.why: That is lifetime, not scope, and locals are not collected: their frame is removed.

prompt: `Blocks.java` fails with `cannot find symbol` for `extra` on line 9. What is the best fix if line 9 really needs the value?
hint: Move the declaration, not the use.

choices.text: Declare `extra` again on line 9
choices.why: A new `extra` would be a different variable with no value from the `if`.

choices.text: Make `extra` a field, so that every method of the class can see it
choices.why: That widens it far beyond what needs it; a field is the opposite of the narrowest block.

choices.text: Declare it before the `if`, so its block is `main`'s
choices.why: Right: then it is in scope on both lines.

prompt: `Twice.java` declares `int total` in `main` and again inside a loop. What happens?
hint: Java's rule for two locals.

choices.text: The inner `total` hides the outer one until the loop ends
choices.why: Some languages do that; Java refuses it for locals.

choices.text: A compile error: `total` is already defined in `main`
choices.why: Right: two locals with one name in overlapping scopes are not allowed.

choices.text: Both are the same variable, so the loop overwrites the outer `total`
choices.why: A declaration always makes a new variable; that is why the compiler objects.

prompt: In `Shadow.java`, after `String name = "Ana";`, how does the program still print the field?
hint: The field is still there, unchanged.

choices.text: It cannot: the local replaced the field for the rest of the program
choices.why: The third line printed `the library`; the field was reachable all along.

choices.text: By naming the class: `Shadow.name`
choices.why: Right: the plain name means the local, and the qualified name means the field.

choices.text: By printing `name` before the local is assigned a new value
choices.why: The local had its value from the start; the first `println` ran before it existed at all.

prompt: Which of these are true of shadowing in Java? Choose all that apply.
hint: A local and a field, or two locals.

choices.text: A local may have the same name as a field
choices.why: Yes: `Shadow.java` compiled and ran.

choices.text: A local may have the same name as another local in an enclosing block
choices.why: No: `Twice.java` was refused.

choices.text: Constructors commonly use it, writing `this.name = name`
choices.why: Yes: lesson 13 writes it that way.

choices.text: The field is deleted from the point where the local is declared
choices.why: It is only hidden from the plain name; `Shadow.name` still reached it.

prompt: When does a local variable stop existing?
hint: It lives in a frame.

choices.text: When the program ends
choices.why: It ends much sooner: with the call that declared it.

choices.text: When the call that declared it returns
choices.why: Right: the frame is removed, and its locals with it.

choices.text: When it is assigned a new value
choices.why: A new value replaces the old one in the same variable; the variable lives on.

prompt: On the default stack, how many frames did `Depth` reach before `StackOverflowError`?
hint: The first two runs agreed.

prompt: With `-Xss256k` `Depth` reached 1,646 frames, and with `-Xss4m` 100,048. Sixteen times the stack gave about sixty times the frames. Why not sixteen?
hint: Not every frame is the same size.

choices.text: `-Xss` is ignored above 1 MB, so the counts are noise
choices.why: It is honoured: 4 MB reached far more than the default.

choices.text: Interpreted and compiled frames differ in size
choices.why: Right: and a longer run compiles more of `dive`; part of the reason is the JIT.

choices.text: Each frame doubles in size as recursion goes deeper
choices.why: A frame holds the same parameter at every level; depth does not grow it.

prompt: A program crashes with `StackOverflowError`. What is the usual right response?
hint: What filled the stack?

choices.text: Raise `-Xss` until it stops
choices.why: A recursion with no way to stop fills any stack; a bigger one only takes longer.

choices.text: Fix the recursion
choices.why: Right: find the recursion that never stops, or stops too late; the fix is in the code.

choices.text: Catch the error everywhere, as `Depth` does
choices.why: `Depth` catches it to print a number for the lesson; catching does not make the recursion end.

choices.text: Give the JVM more heap with `-Xmx`
choices.why: Frames are on the stack, not the heap; `-Xmx` sizes the heap.

prompt: A method creates an object with `new`, keeps a reference in a local, and returns that reference. After it returns, what is left?
hint: Where does each live?

choices.text: Nothing: the object was in the frame and went with it
choices.why: Objects are on the heap, not in frames; only the local went.

choices.text: The local and the object, until the program ends
choices.why: The local went with the frame; only the object outlives the call.

choices.text: Only the object, on the heap; the local went with its frame
choices.why: Right: the frame disappeared and the object stayed on the heap.

prompt: A method declares `int count;` and reads it at once. Another declares a field `static int count;` and reads it at once. What happens in each?
hint: One rule for locals, one for fields.

choices.text: Both print 0, the default every `int` starts with
choices.why: The local is refused at compile time; only the field gets a default.

choices.text: The local is a compile error, and the field prints its default, 0
choices.why: Right: locals need definite assignment, fields start at their default.

choices.text: Both are compile errors, since neither was assigned
choices.why: The field compiles: `Defaults.java` printed its zeros.

prompt: `main` calls `a`, and `a` calls `b`. Put the frames in the order they leave the stack.
hint: The last in is the first out.

prompt: A colleague declares every variable at the top of `main`, "so they are all visible". What does that cost, by this lesson's rules?
hint: Think about scope as protection.

choices.text: Nothing: scope only matters to the compiler
choices.why: Scope also limits where a value can be misused, which is what is lost.

choices.text: Memory, because every variable then lives until the program ends
choices.why: They live until `main` returns, which is the same for a block inside `main`; memory is not the point.

choices.text: Every variable is exposed far from where it is needed
choices.why: Right: declared in the narrowest block, a variable cannot leak outside it.

prompt: A method that calls itself is using ___.
hint: `dive` did it.
